newsitem.title: DENMARK: FOCUS - Denmark says economy strong, warns on wages.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Denmark says economy strong, warns on wages.

text.p: Denmark's economy ministry gave the country a clean bill of financial health in its latest set of forecasts on Tuesday but said that it could still catch cold if next spring's pay round produced excessive demands.

The report said that increased estimates for 1996 Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth, the current account balance, employment, exports and consumption did not signal an increased danger of overheating.
"Data received since our October survey does not point to any growing risk of overheating but it does mean that greater surveillance will be needed," it said.

The survey left unaltered its October forecast of average public sector pay rises of 2.6 percent in 1997 with wages in private industry seen increasing by 4.0 percent, growth that Economy Minister Marianne Jelved said was too high.
"The target is that our rate of wage increases should be no more than that which we see abroad," she told a news conference.
The report said that pay rises in accordance with its forecast would give a rate of increase 1.5 percentage point higher than the average expected in core European Union states.
"Pay in Denmark is rising at a somewhat higher level than in our most important trading partners. This could put the current account surplus and employment at risk," Jelved said.
"The government calls upon the employers and unions to negotiate pay deals which will ensure that the number of jobless can go on falling," she added.
Jelved said that the Danish government intended to continue its policies of moderate fiscal tightening in 1998, stressing the need to cut foreign debt of around 250 billion crowns ($42 billion).
"Denmark's foreign debt is still far too big and so it is necessary that we can go on posting solid current account surpluses," she said.
The ministry's forecast saw the current account surplus rising to 15.0 billion crowns in 1998 from 12.0 billion this year and 13.0 billion next year.
Unemployment was seen falling to 7.6 percent of the workforce in 1998 from an expected 8.8 percent in 1996 and 8.0 percent in 1997.
The survey raised government expectations for 1996 GDP growth to 2.2 percent from 2.0 percent in its previous, October, forecast but lowered its 1997 prognosis to 2.9 percent from 3.1 percent.

It maintained its inflation forecasts of 2.1 percent in 1996 and 2.3 percent in 1997 and saw the public sector budget going from a 16.7 billion crown deficit in 1996 to a 2.0 billion crown surplus in 1997, rising to 4.8 billion in 1998.
"The good development in the Danish economy gives cause for optimism but if we are to continue to make advances, we must not squander these good results," Jelved said.
Bond yields, increasingly seen by market analysts to be at the bottom of the current cycle, were unlikely to move for the next two years, the report said.
It saw the 10-year benchmark yielding 6.7 percent at the end of 1997 and 6.6 percent in December 1998. On Tuesday it stood at 6.65 percent.
